studies.title: Secretly Sending Affection
studies.meaning: The address is to believers and the subject is a private act, not a public alliance. Affection is being sent quietly to people who had expelled the community, and the ayah names both the sending and the concealing. Its argument runs on a mismatch: those addressed had left everything for a cause, and are now leaking warmth back towards what they left. Two clauses about God knowing the hidden and the declared close the gap the secrecy assumed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators report with broad agreement that a man of the community sent a private letter to Mecca warning of a coming expedition, and that his motive was to protect relatives still living there rather than to betray anyone. He was found out, questioned, and pardoned. The occasion is unusually well attested, and the ayah addresses the act while the surrounding passage widens it into a general principle.

keyTerms.note: From a root for love that seeks the good of its object and expresses itself in acts. It is the warmest word in this field, which is why its use here makes the passage about feeling rather than about treaties.
A verb for confiding something under the breath. The ayah uses an open verb for the same act one clause earlier and this hidden one here, so the two describe the same warmth at different volumes.
Literally the evenness of the way, a road without a rise or a dip in it. Straying from it is not described as choosing a different road but as leaving the smooth part of this one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Almost everyone in Medina who had come from Mecca still had family there: a mother, a brother, sons who had not left. Caravans went back and forth constantly, and a letter could travel with any trader for the price of a meal. Keeping a line open to relatives was not exotic conduct; it was what any decent man in that society would have thought he owed his own blood.
studies.didYouKnow: The definite form of the word for affection used in this ayah occurs only here in the Quran. Six ayat later, the indefinite form of the same word appears as something God may yet place between the two sides. The surah warns against sending it and then holds out the possibility of its arrival, using one root for both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes an inward state seriously as a matter of consequence, which is different from policing an opinion. What is described is not a belief but a direction of loyalty expressed in an act, and the act had a cost measurable in lives. Naming both concealment and disclosure in one clause removes the category of a private exception, which is exactly what the person addressed had assumed existed.

crossReferences.why: Draws the boundary of this passage seven ayat later, exempting those who never fought or expelled anyone.
Holds out the possibility of affection between the two sides, which keeps this passage from being permanent.
Warns against taking intimates from outside who never cease to wish the community harm.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have done recently that you would not want a particular person to know about, and ask why. Sometimes the answer is ordinary privacy, which is fine. Sometimes it is that you know the two halves of your life would not survive being introduced. This ayah is only about the second kind.

studies.title: Hands And Tongues Together
studies.meaning: A short ayah supplies the evidence the previous one assumed. If they get the upper hand, three things follow: they act as enemies, they stretch out hands and tongues with harm, and they wish for the community's faith to collapse. The pairing of hands and tongues is exact, covering violence and speech as one category. The last clause moves from conduct to desire, which is what makes the description reach past any particular incident.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, supporting the instruction of the previous ayah with a statement about conduct. The community's memory of Mecca was recent and specific: years of pressure before the migration, and hostility that had continued afterwards. The commentators read this ayah as supplying the reason rather than reporting a fresh incident, and the conditional opening keeps it about what happens when circumstances allow rather than about a fixed nature.

keyTerms.note: A verb for coming upon someone and having them within reach, occurring only here in the Quran. It describes opportunity rather than intention, which is why the ayah is conditional rather than absolute.
The ordinary verb for spreading a hand open, used elsewhere of generosity. Applying it to harm is deliberate: the same gesture that gives is the one that reaches to strike.
From the same root as the word for affection this passage has just used. The surah puts warmth and hostile wishing on one root, so the contrast is between two directions of the same faculty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tongue could do more damage than a hand in Arabia. Satirical verse was a weapon of war, composed to be memorised and repeated at wells and markets until a man's name was ruined in every camp he might need. Tribes retained poets the way they retained warriors. Naming hands and tongues in one breath was not a figure of speech; it listed the two instruments an enemy actually used.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for getting hold of someone in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. The verb for wishing that closes it comes from the same root as the word for affection in the previous ayah, so within two ayat the identical root names both the warmth being sent and the harm being wished back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The conditional form matters. The ayah does not say these people are incapable of anything else; it says what happens when they have the advantage, which is a claim about circumstance and character together. That leaves the door open that the surah walks through five ayat later. Ending on what they wish rather than what they do also locates the real difficulty in a place no treaty can reach.

crossReferences.why: Answers the condition described here by holding out affection between the two sides as possible.
Uses the same reasoning about people whose hatred has already shown in what their mouths let slip.
Says that whenever they overcome you they respect neither kinship nor treaty, the same conditional form.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between what someone has actually done to you and what you believe they would do if they could. Both may be true, but only the first is evidence. Write the two lists separately once this week for a person you find difficult. The separation usually shortens one of them considerably.

studies.title: Where The Ties Are Cut
studies.meaning: The ayah answers the motive the whole passage has been circling. The letter was written for relatives; here the relatives are named and set aside, together with children, at the one point where the account is settled. The verb chosen is not about abandonment but about separation, a cutting between people who arrive together. The closing name for God's sight returns the reader to the present, where the conduct is happening and being seen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage responding to a letter sent to Mecca out of concern for family. The commentators emphasise that the motive was kinship rather than disbelief, which is why the answer addresses kinship directly. Arab society organised protection, inheritance and standing entirely through blood, so an argument that relatives will not help had to be made explicitly. It could not be assumed.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for a womb, used as the ordinary Arabic term for kin. Naming relatives by the organ that produced them keeps the tie physical, which is what makes its cancellation here striking.
A verb for making a clean division, used of separating two things that were joined and of giving a decisive verdict. Both senses are live here, since the separating and the judging are one act.

An intensive form from the root for sight, but in Arabic it covers insight as much as vision. It names someone who sees and also understands what is seen, which is why it closes an ayah about motives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's womb-relations were his insurance policy. They paid compensation when he killed by accident, avenged him when he was killed, took in his widow, and fed his children in a famine year. There was no other institution doing any of that. Telling someone in that society that kin would not benefit him was not a moral observation; it was a claim about the failure of the only safety net there was.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for kinship in this ayah is the plural of the word for a womb, and it shares its root with the two names of God that open almost every surah of the Quran. The same three letters carry both the tie set aside here and the divine mercy named at the head of the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say kinship is worthless; it says it does not transfer. That is a precise limit, and it leaves every duty towards relatives intact while removing the idea that they can stand in for a person. What follows is a kind of moral solitude that the Quran states plainly rather than softening. And the sentence about separation is in the active voice, so the parting is done rather than merely happening.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same relations one by one at the moment each person has enough to preoccupy him.
Says no parent will avail his child and no child his parent in anything on that Day.
Places goodness to relatives among the standing obligations, which this ayah does not cancel.

studies.applyIt: Do one thing for a relative this week that has nothing to do with obligation or appearances, and do not tell anyone you did it. This ayah limits what family can do for you at the end. It does not limit what you can do for them now, and the two are easier to hold apart than people expect.

studies.title: An Excellent Example, With One Exception
studies.meaning: A model is offered and then immediately qualified. Abraham and those with him declared themselves quit of their people's worship, and the declaration is quoted in full, including a hard clause about enmity lasting until belief. Then one thing is excepted: his promise to seek forgiveness for his father. The exception is not a criticism of Abraham but a marking of what is not part of the pattern. The passage closes on his prayer of reliance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, offering a precedent to a community torn between conviction and family in Mecca. Abraham was the ancestor the Arabs of the Hijaz claimed, which made him the one figure both sides of the conflict honoured. The commentators note that the exception about his father is explained elsewhere in the Quran, where the promise is described as made on account of a pledge and later withdrawn.

keyTerms.note: A pattern one shapes oneself by, not merely an admirable story. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, twice in this surah of Abraham and once of the Prophet.
A noun for settled aversion rather than a flash of anger. It is paired here with the word for enmity, so the phrase covers both the feeling and the state of hostility it produces.

A verb for turning towards someone repeatedly, used of a person coming back again and again. It is gentler than the usual word for repentance and suggests a direction of travel rather than a single act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every tribe in the Hijaz traced itself to an ancestor and recited the line at gatherings. Abraham stood at the head of that reckoning for the Arabs of Mecca, and the sanctuary they administered was associated with him. Invoking him was not reaching for a distant figure from another people's scripture. It was naming the founder both parties claimed, and asking which of them was actually following him.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for an excellent example occurs three times in the whole Quran. Two of the three are in this surah, at this ayah and two ayat later, both about Abraham and those with him. The third, at 33:21, uses the identical wording of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting an exception inside a model is unusual and consequential. It says that a figure can be exemplary without every recorded act being exemplary, which protects the reader from a flattening kind of imitation. It also preserves something tender: the promise excepted is a son's promise to a father, and the Quran does not condemn the impulse behind it. What is marked is that the promise could not be kept, not that it was wrong to feel.

crossReferences.why: Explains the excepted promise, describing it as made on account of a pledge and then set aside.
Gives the words of the promise itself, spoken as Abraham withdraws from his father's household.
Uses the identical phrase for an excellent example, there of the messenger rather than of Abraham.

studies.applyIt: Take one person you admire and name a single thing about them you would not copy. Not to diminish them, but because the exercise makes the admiration usable. This ayah does exactly that with the most honoured figure it could have chosen, and it does it in the same sentence as the praise.

studies.title: Do Not Make Us A Test
studies.meaning: The prayer asks for something indirect. Not for safety or victory, but that the community not become a trial for those who reject faith. Commentators read this two ways: that the believers not be defeated in a manner that hardens the other side, and that they not be made an instrument by which others are tested and fail. Both readings put the concern outside the person praying. Forgiveness is asked for second, and two names close it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the words attributed to Abraham and those with him and offered to the community as a pattern. The situation being addressed is one where believers were a visible minority whose fortunes were read by others as evidence about their claims. The commentators connect the prayer to that exposure rather than to a specific incident, and it is given here as words to be borrowed.

keyTerms.note: From a root for putting metal in fire to separate the pure from the dross. The word covers testing, temptation and civil strife at once, which is why the classical readings of this line diverge.
A verb for placing something into a condition or a role. The prayer does not ask to be spared a feeling; it asks not to be positioned in a particular way relative to other people.

From a root for covering something protectively, which also gives the word for a helmet. Forgiveness in this vocabulary is a covering placed over a fault rather than a declaration that nothing happened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation moved between tribes as reliable news. When a small group prospered, the story travelled that its gods or its luck were sound; when it was broken, the same route carried the opposite conclusion. Nobody in that world separated the fate of a community from the truth of what it claimed. A prayer about not becoming other people's evidence was a prayer about a mechanism everyone could see working.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a trial in this prayer appears in ten ayat of the Quran, and its root describes the assaying of metal by fire. At 25:20 the same word is used of people being made a trial for one another, which is the exact position this prayer asks not to be placed in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer's structure says something about how faith relates to reputation. It does not ask that the community be spared hardship, and it does not ask that the other side be defeated. It asks that whatever happens should not become an argument against God in someone else's mouth. That places a believer's concern outside their own outcome, which is a demanding place to put it and an unusual one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for people made a trial for one another, and asks whether they will be patient.
Records the same request in the mouths of Moses' people, using the identical phrasing.
Supplies the declaration these words conclude, spoken by Abraham and those with him.

studies.applyIt: Before your next difficult conversation, add one line to whatever you were going to ask for: that however this goes, it should not make things harder for someone watching. It is a small shift and it changes what you are willing to say. This prayer is asking for exactly that, and it asks it first.

studies.title: Perhaps Affection, Later
studies.meaning: The example is restated and its audience narrowed to whoever hopes for God and the Last Day, which makes the pattern conditional on an orientation rather than on membership. Then two names arrive for whoever turns away, one saying God needs nothing and one saying He is praised regardless. The second ayah changes the temperature entirely. Using a particle of possibility rather than promise, it holds out affection between the two sides, and closes on capability and forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and events in the years that followed gave the second ayah a history. Many of those the community was in conflict with at Mecca later entered the same community, and the commentators cite that development when reading this passage. The ayah itself makes no forecast. It is placed at the end of a hard instruction about loyalty, and it changes what that instruction is understood to be for.

keyTerms.note: A particle of hope and expectation, not of promise. Its presence keeps the ayah from predicting anything, which is what allows it to be read at a moment when reconciliation looks impossible.

From the root for wealth and needing nothing further. Applied to God after a mention of people turning away, it removes any suggestion that a departure costs Him something, which would make the instruction self-interested.
The indefinite form of the word the surah opened by warning against sending. It occurs three times in the Quran, once here and once of the affection God places between a husband and wife.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia ran for generations, and everyone knew examples that had outlasted the memory of what started them. They also knew how such things ended: not by argument but by a marriage, a payment, or one strong man deciding it was over. Reconciliation was a normal event in that world, arranged rather than felt, and the affection usually arrived afterwards if it arrived at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for affection here occurs three times in the Quran. One of the others, at 30:21, names the affection God places between spouses as a sign; the third, at 5:82, identifies those nearest in affection to the believers. The same noun therefore covers marriage, unexpected friendship, and a hoped-for end to hostility.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a possibility of affection at the end of an instruction about hostility does real work. It marks the hostility as answering a situation rather than describing a permanent order, and it puts the change outside human management by making God the one who might place it. That combination asks something specific of a reader: to act on present facts without concluding anything about a person's future.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the affection placed between spouses, and calls it a sign.
Opens the surah by warning against sending that same affection, which this ayah reopens as a possibility.
Names people nearest in affection to the believers, showing the category is not fixed in advance.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship you have written off as finished and, without contacting anyone, hold it open in your mind as a thing that might change. Not likely. Possible. This ayah uses a particle that means only that much, and it puts it at the end of the harshest passage in the surah.
